claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has microstructural heterogeneities in grain size, dislocation density, and impurity distribution.
Controlled thermal annealing will homogenize the microstructure of Q235 steel.
Annealing will reduce grain-boundary heterogeneity and dislocation density in Q235 steel.
Microstructural uniformity governs the formation and adherence of a protective oxide scale.
A homogenized microstructure enables more uniform diffusion and oxidation at high temperature.
Uniform high-temperature oxidation produces a continuous, robust oxide film.
A continuous and adherent oxide film prevents localized corrosion and improves hot-corrosion resistance.
A heterogeneous microstructure causes uneven oxidation and weak points at which the oxide scale breaks down.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, annealed Q235 steel will have lower weight change than as-received Q235 steel.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, annealed Q235 steel will form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale than as-received Q235 steel.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, annealed Q235 steel will have a lower corrosion rate than as-received Q235 steel.
Untreated Q235 steel will form a non-uniform oxide scale and undergo greater corrosion-related weight change at high temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily in aggressive salt environments at 700–900 °C where oxidation dynamics dominate.
The benefit of annealing will be significantly diminished or qualitatively different at room temperature.
Salt composition, exposure duration, and minor compositional deviations in Q235 steel may alter the observed corrosion response.
Comparing identically exposed annealed and as-received Q235 samples, with room-temperature controls, is intended to isolate the effect of annealing.

Failure of annealed samples to show statistically significant improvements in weight change, oxide-scale continuity and adherence, and corrosion rate under high-temperature salt exposure would falsify the hypothesis.
